\subsection{Reconstructed scoring and the query-only constant}

With $\gamma=2\langle\widehat p,\widehat r\rangle$, real-arithmetic expansion gives
\begin{align}
 \refineddist(q,x)
 &=\primarydist(q,x)+\|q'-\widehat r(x)\|_2^2+\gamma(x)
 \label{eq:5-refined-score}\\
 &=2\|q'\|_2^2+\|\widehat p+\widehat r\|_2^2-2\langle q',\widehat p+\widehat r\rangle\nonumber\\
 &=\|q'-\widehat p(x)-\widehat r(x)\|_2^2+\|q'\|_2^2.
 \label{eq:5-refined-constant}
\end{align}
The query-only constant preserves ranking; reconstruction error remains \cite{jhq}.

The scalar path sums squared coordinate differences between $q'$ and residual reconstruction, then adds the primary score/correction. Queries and fitting codebooks use shared memory.

For $\lrefine=L\in\{1,8,16,32\}$,
\[
 d_{\rm word}=32/B_R,\qquad
 \text{words of lane }a:\ a,a+L,a+2L,\ldots.
\]
A word holds four eight-bit or eight four-bit codes. Butterfly shuffles sum lane partials; lane zero writes the score.

\[

\subsection{A complete-key upper bound with explicit witnesses}

Let $K_{(c)}$ be the global $c$th key when $|U|\geq c$. If a group holds
$c$ distinct, fully scored candidates, the largest key among those
witnesses, $\tau_j$, satisfies $K_{(c)}\preceq\tau_j$. There are already
$c$ candidates no later than $\tau_j$ in the global universe. The shared
bound is initialised to a top sentinel and updated by
\begin{equation}
 \tau\leftarrow\min_{\prec}(\tau,\tau_j).
 \label{eq:5-shared-update}
\end{equation}
No bound is published from fewer than $c$ valid candidates. If the entire
universe has fewer than $c$, no group can publish such a bound and all
valid candidates remain eligible.

\begin{resultblock}
\begin{proposition}[Safe rejection by a witnessed bound]
\label{prop:5-shared-bound}
Assume fixed keys, publications backed by $c$ distinct candidates, and
reads that return either the initial sentinel or one complete published
key. Rejecting a candidate only when $K_q(x)\succ\tau$ cannot remove a
global top-$c$ candidate, irrespective of publication timing.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A publication has a set $W_\tau$ of $c$ distinct witnesses:
\[
 \max_{x\in W_\tau}K_q(x)\preceq\tau
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad K_{(c)}\preceq\tau.
\]
Sentinel reads and minima of published keys obey the same inequality. Thus
\[
 x\in\operatorname{Top}_c(U)
 \ \Longrightarrow\ K_q(x)\preceq K_{(c)}\preceq\tau_{\rm seen}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ x\text{ is not rejected}.
\]
Stale reads only loosen the bound. Publications
made after earlier safe rejections remain valid: any $c$ retained
distinct candidates still supply $c$ witnesses, whether or not they are
the best $c$ of their group.
\end{proof}
\end{resultblock}

A shared bound may discard local winners while preserving \cref{prop:5-local-coverage}'s global coverage. Admission is
\begin{equation}
 K_q(x)\prec\lambda_j
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 K_q(x)\preceq\tau_{\rm seen},
 \label{eq:5-admission}
\end{equation}
Here $\lambda_j$ is the local compaction threshold and $\tau_{\rm seen}$ the last shared key read. Equality with the shared bound stays eligible.

\subsection{Publication, filtering and implementation limits}

For nonnegative FP32 scores, canonical positive zero and valid nonnegative positions,
\begin{equation}
 \kappa(D,p)=2^{32}\operatorname{uintbits}_{32}(D)+p.
 \label{eq:5-packed-key}
\end{equation}
Non-NaN float bits are increasing on this domain, so
\[
 (D_1,p_1)\prec(D_2,p_2)\iff\kappa(D_1,p_1)<\kappa(D_2,p_2).
\]
Infinity follows finite scores; the all-one sentinel follows valid keys. Invalid positions cannot publish.

\subsection{Choosing parallelism without changing the budget}

Grouping launches $b\gscan$ blocks, adding parallelism, staging, selection and merging. Smaller quotas need a certificate/fallback. Concentrated pilot survivors motivated witnessed bounds (\cref{sec:7-4}).

Let $T_{\rm blk}$ be scan threads per block, $H$ the number of SMs times
the maximum resident threads per SM, and
$v=\operatorname{sd}(n_c)/\operatorname{mean}(n_c)$ the candidate-count
coefficient of variation. Its rule is
\begin{align}
 g_{\rm fill}
 &=\max\!\left(\{1\}\cup
       \{h\in\{2,4,8\}:bhT_{\rm blk}\leq0.6H\}\right),
       \label{eq:5-fill-rule}\\
 g_{\rm skew}&=
   \begin{cases}4,&v\geq0.3,\\1,&v<0.3,\end{cases}
 \qquad
 g_{\rm chosen}=\max(g_{\rm fill},g_{\rm skew}).
 \label{eq:5-skew-rule}
\end{align}
The skew rule may override the fill limit. In the evaluation harness,
$v$ is calibrated using 512 database vectors as pseudoqueries and a
fixed routing configuration; it uses no ground-truth labels. This is
distinct from Chapter 6's sampled output-agreement calibration. Once
calibrated, scheduling uses the batch size and stored statistic without
an additional per-search host readback. The constants were fitted on
four pilot configurations and then evaluated on further configurations.
The one-time pseudoquery calibration is excluded from
the reported steady-state search times. Observed startup ranges, separate from refinement-budget calibration (\cref{sec:a-supplement}), are
\[

 T_{\rm first}\in[6.00,27.77]\,\mathrm{ms},\quad
 \operatorname{median}(T_{\rm repeat})\in[2.72,18.13]\,\mathrm{ms}.
\]

Choosing one group dispatches $\gscan=0$ at fixed index/probes/budget. Its distance-only ties need a common-order check for identical survivors. Integrated gains/regret are in \cref{sec:7-6}.

\subsection{Address mapping and four-byte packing}

For list $\ell$, row $r$ maps to
\[
 p=o_\ell+r,\qquad \operatorname{offset}(Z[m,p])=mN+p.
\]
At fixed $m$, adjacent positions have adjacent bytes. Crossing lists can still cause a jump.

A word packs four subspaces of one candidate:
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf{w}[j,p]=\sum_{t=0}^{3}2^{8t}Z[4j+t,p],\qquad
 \operatorname{offset}_{\rm bytes}(\mathsf{w}[j,p])=4(jN+p).
 \label{eq:5-packed-layout}
\end{equation}
For $0\leq t<4$ and eight-bit $Z$,
\[
 (\mathsf w[j,p]\gg8t)\mathbin{\&}255=Z[4j+t,p].
\]
The recovered nibbles index \cref{eq:5-lut-factorisation}.

\subsection{What is inherited}

JHQ combines rotation and a primary/residual hierarchy \cite{jhq}. For square $\Pi\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$,
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 \Pi^\top\Pi=I
 &\Longrightarrow
 \|\Pi(q-x)\|^2\\
 &=(q-x)^\top\Pi^\top\Pi(q-x)=\|q-x\|^2.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:2-isometry}
\end{equation}
Dimension remains $d$. This is a real-arithmetic identity; quantisation, FP32 orthogonality and GEMM error are separate checks.

Partition $y$ into $M$ subspaces of dimension $D_s=d/M$. With $B$ bits per
primary subspace, $K=2^B$ labels are formed from $L=2^{B/D_s}$ scalar levels,
requiring the implemented Cartesian parameters to make $L$ an integer.
Writing $\Phi$ for the standard normal CDF, the constructor uses
\begin{equation}
 a_i=\sigma\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{i-1/2}{L}\right),\quad
 i=1,\ldots,L,\qquad
 \mathcal C_m=\{a_1,\ldots,a_L\}^{D_s}.
 \label{eq:2-cartesian}
\end{equation}
At the evaluated $B=D_s=8$, $L=2$ and $\mathcal C_m=\{-a,+a\}^8$,
with $a\simeq0.67449\sigma$. Each byte records eight coordinate signs.
The implementation estimates $\sigma$ from vector energy; unit-normalised
inputs motivate the scale $1/\sqrt d$. This representation is prior art,
not an invention of the GPU execution layer.

Residuals are $r=y-\widehat p$, giving reconstruction $\widehat y=\widehat p+\widehat r$. The evaluated codes use $d/8$ primary bytes and $d$ residual bytes per vector, before metadata. Refining fewer rows reduces reads, not stored residual size.

\subsection{Model assumptions and score semantics}

Random rotation can spread coordinate energy, motivating a shared
Gaussian-inspired scalar model. It does not force an arbitrary realised
database to have independent, zero-mean Gaussian coordinates. For a fixed
rotation and empirical database mean $\mu$, the transformed mean is
$\Pi\mu$ and $\|\Pi\mu\|=\|\mu\|$. Averaging over random rotations is
different from centring one fixed corpus. Even a uniformly random point on
a sphere has dependent coordinates through its fixed norm. Consequently,
isometry is an algebraic guarantee; the distributional approximation is a
modelling assumption. Chapter 8's centred-coding pilot examines one practical
consequence of that distinction.

The inherited primary levels are Gaussian mid-quantiles. For $X\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$ and a zero threshold,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 a_{\rm MSE}

\subsection{Candidate partition and deterministic ordering}

For a fixed query, concatenate the selected inverted lists in probe order
to obtain $n_c$ candidate occurrences. Assume that each visited database
row occurs once and that the index stays fixed during search. For
$\gscan\in\{1,2,4,8\}$, block $(q,j)$ owns the interval
\begin{equation}
 U_j=\left[\left\lfloor\frac{j n_c}{\gscan}\right\rfloor,
              \left\lfloor\frac{(j+1)n_c}{\gscan}\right\rfloor\right),
 \qquad j=0,\ldots,\gscan-1.
 \label{eq:5-partition}
\end{equation}
Here an interval denotes the corresponding candidates, rather than their
database IDs. The device computes its endpoints from the routed candidate
count. Groups differ in size by at most one candidate; a long list can
cross a group boundary. This balances candidate counts, whereas assigning
equal numbers of lists need not do so. Each thread finds its first list
through the probe-prefix offsets and advances its list cursor while
scanning its interval. Residual codes are not read at this stage.

The selection key is
\begin{equation}
 K_q(x)=\bigl(\primarydist(q,x),p(x)\bigr),
 \qquad
 (a,p)\prec(b,r)\iff a<b\ \text{or}\ (a=b\ \text{and}\ p<r),
 \label{eq:5-primary-key}
\end{equation}
where $p(x)$ is the physical row position in the fixed inverted-list
storage. It is unique among the query's candidates and independent of
the order of atomic appends. It is not the database ID used to break
final-result ties. With non-NaN scores, this defines a total order on
distinct candidates. Local selection and merging use this order. Partition independence also requires identical computed scores across paths.

\subsection{Exact local retention and global coverage}

$\operatorname{Top}_c(V)$ contains the first $\min(c,|V|)$ keys, where $c=\max\{k,\lceil\alpha k\rceil\}$. Each group keeps up to $c$, since all global winners may lie there; a $c/\gscan$ quota is unsafe.

\begin{resultblock}
\begin{lemma}[Local-buffer retention]
\label{lem:5-buffer}
Let $V_t$ be the candidates scored by a block through chunk $t$, and
$B_t$ its valid buffer after any compaction or filtering at that point.
Assume fixed complete keys, sufficient append capacity and exact
top-$c$ compaction. Let $\beta_t$ be the minimum of the complete shared
bounds observed so far, including the initial top sentinel. Then
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{Top}_c(V_t)\cap\{x:K_q(x)\preceq\beta_t\}
 \subseteq B_t.
 \label{eq:5-buffer-invariant}
\end{equation}
With sharing disabled, the bound is the sentinel and the buffer contains
the whole prefix top-$c$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The empty prefix is immediate. Put
\[
 E_t=\operatorname{Top}_c(V_t)\cap\{x:K_q(x)\preceq\beta_t\}.
\]
On extending $V_t$ to $V_{t+1}$, $\beta_{t+1}\preceq\beta_t$ and
\[
 \operatorname{Top}_c(V_{t+1})\cap V_t\subseteq\operatorname{Top}_c(V_t).
\]
Hence every old member of $E_{t+1}$ was retained. A locally rejected new key has $c$ earlier predecessors, so cannot enter the new prefix top-$c$. All other eligible arrivals fit by the capacity assumption. For any eligible winner $x$,
\[
 \#\{y\in B:K_q(y)\prec K_q(x)\}
 \leq\#\{y\in V_{t+1}:K_q(y)\prec K_q(x)\}<c,
\]
so exact compaction keeps $x$. Filtering removes only keys above an observed bound; their running minimum covers stale reads. These steps preserve the invariant inductively.
\end{proof}
\end{resultblock}

\begin{resultblock}
\begin{proposition}[Coverage and truncated merging]
\label{prop:5-local-coverage}
For fixed keys under a common total order, let $U$ be the visited
universe and $V$ any retained subset. If
$\operatorname{Top}_c(U)\subseteq V\subseteq U$, then
$\operatorname{Top}_c(V)=\operatorname{Top}_c(U)$.
Pairwise sorted merging with truncation to $c$ preserves this result.
In particular, for disjoint groups,
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{Top}_c\!\left(\bigcup_j U_j\right)
 =\operatorname{Top}_c\!\left(\bigcup_j
                    \operatorname{Top}_c(U_j)\right).
 \label{eq:5-topc-union}
\end{equation}
The statement includes universes smaller than $c$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every global winner is in $V$, and every other member of $V$ follows
the global winners. Selection from $V$ therefore recovers them.
For the independent-group special case, let $x$ belong to the global
top-$c$ and to group $U_j$. Fewer than $c$
candidates precede $x$ globally, so fewer than $c$ precede it within $U_j$.
Consequently $x\in\operatorname{Top}_c(U_j)$, and the local union contains
every global winner. Selecting its first $c$ therefore recovers precisely
the global winners in the same order. If the whole universe has fewer
than $c$ members, every member is retained.

For merging, the first $c$ of two sorted lists are their union's
top-$c$. A discarded candidate already has at least $c$ predecessors
within that union and cannot enter the top-$c$ of any larger union.
Induction over the merge tree establishes the claim.
\end{proof}
\end{resultblock}

\subsection{Merge implementation, storage and boundary cases}

At $\gscan>1$, a 256-thread block merges each query over $\log_2\gscan$ rounds. Each pair emits $\min(c,a+b)$ entries using Merge Path slices \cite{gpu_merge_path}.
All comparisons use \cref{eq:5-primary-key}; block barriers separate
rounds. \Cref{fig:5-global-selection} illustrates the truncation invariant.
The tree emits at most $c(\gscan-1)$ key pairs across its internal nodes,
in addition to the partition searches and synchronisation work.

The two global score/position workspaces have capacities
$[b_{\rm cap},\gscan,c]$ and $[b_{\rm cap},\gscan/2,c]$ and alternate between
rounds. With four-byte scores and positions, their combined payload is
\begin{equation}
 S_{\rm pairs}=8b_{\rm cap}c\left(\gscan+\frac{\gscan}{2}\right)
 \quad\text{bytes},\qquad \gscan>1.
 \label{eq:5-group-workspace}
\end{equation}
Counts add $4b_{\rm cap}\gscan$ bytes and provisioned bounds add $8b_{\rm cap}$, beyond survivor/other workspace. Allocation grows before capture and stays reserved for reuse. Merging stages lengths, not all keys, in shared memory.

Valid counts exclude padding:
\[
 K_{\rm sort\ pad}=(+\infty,\mathrm{INT\_MAX}),\qquad
 K_{\rm output\ pad}=(+\infty,-1).
\]
Valid positions are below $\mathrm{INT\_MAX}$; empty groups have count zero. Refinement skips negative positions, and merges exclude them. At $\gscan=1$, survivors go directly to output.

$\gscan=0$ uses one block per query with distance-exact selection and free cutoff-tie IDs. Lossy \texttt{K\_LOCAL=4} requires \texttt{JHQ\_EXACT\_TOPCK=0}; paper-faithful builds disable it.

For nonempty scanned set $V$, let $h=\min(c,|V|)$ and $d_h$ be its $h$th score. Distance-only compaction yields
\[
 \{x:d_x<d_h\}\subseteq B\subseteq\{x:d_x\leq d_h\},\qquad |B|=h.
\]
A rejection has $c$ witnesses with no larger score; only tied identities remain free. T4 checks this contract and grouped full-key order by CPU sorting GPU-produced scores (\cref{sec:7-strict-selection}).

Write $z=16h+l$, with $h,l\in\{0,\ldots,15\}$ and $\mathcal C_m[z]=(A_m[h],B_m[l])$. Then

Coordinate separation gives
\begin{equation}
 T_m[z]=T_m^{\rm hi}[z\!\gg\!4]
        +T_m^{\rm lo}[z\mathbin{\&}15].
 \label{eq:5-lut-factorisation}
\end{equation}
Storage falls to $16+16=32$ entries; codes, candidates and real-arithmetic scores stay fixed.

Probe selection precedes primary scanning and selects inverted lists,
not database-vector survivors. For IVF centroid $\mu_i$, the selector
orders the FP32-valued computed routing scores
\begin{equation}
 s_i=\|\mu_i\|_2^2-2\langle q',\mu_i\rangle,
 \qquad (s_i,i)\ \text{ordered lexicographically}.
 \label{eq:5-probe-score}
\end{equation}
Omitting the common query norm preserves centroid ordering. In contrast
to primary squared-distance tables, these scores can be negative. The
required output is the first $n_{\rm sel}=\min(n_{\rm probe},n_{\rm list})$
centroid IDs in score order, using the smaller list ID at a tie, plus
the prefix offsets of their list lengths.

OpenAI rotation and centroid GEMMs use TF32 inputs with FP32 accumulation in v69. Probe selection is exact on these computed scores; later FP32 \texttt{fma} retains GEMM rounding (\cref{sec:7-precision}).

\subsection{Radix selection followed by deterministic ordering}

One block makes four radix passes, most-significant byte first. Each histogram counts the chosen prefix; its selected bin updates the residual rank. Four bytes determine the cutoff and required equal-key count.

Canonicalise signed zeros to positive zero, then map bits $u$ by
\begin{equation}
 F(u)=\begin{cases}
       \mathop{\sim}u,&\text{if the sign bit is set},\\
       u\mathbin{|}2^{31},&\text{otherwise}.
      \end{cases}
 \label{eq:5-probe-key}
\end{equation}
For non-NaN scores, monotonicity follows by cases:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 D_1<D_2<0&\Rightarrow u_1>u_2\Rightarrow{\sim}u_1<{\sim}u_2,\\
 0\leq D_1<D_2&\Rightarrow u_1<u_2\Rightarrow
 (u_1\mathbin{|}2^{31})<(u_2\mathbin{|}2^{31}),\\
 D_1<0\leq D_2&\Rightarrow F(u_1)<2^{31}\leq F(u_2).
 \end{aligned}
\]
This covers infinities and equal zeros, unlike \cref{eq:5-packed-key}'s nonnegative-only domain. Every pass uses the same rounded \texttt{fma}, fixing recomputed keys.

Histogram storage is
\[
 256\ \text{bins}\times32\ \text{lane replicas}\times4\ \text{bytes}=32\,\mathrm{KiB}.
\]
Replicas separate same-warp updates, with inter-warp contention and reduction overhead remaining.

Let $h$ be the cutoff key. Collection forms
\[
 A_< =\{i:F(u_i)<h\},\quad A_= =\{i:F(u_i)=h\},\quad
 m=n_{\rm sel}-|A_<|.
\]
It takes $A_< $ and the $m$ smallest list IDs from $A_=$. Ballots/prefix counts enforce this order, independent of atomic arrival. For the resulting set $A$,
\[
 \operatorname{rank}(i)=|\{j\in A:(s_j,j)\prec(s_i,i)\}|,
 \qquad\mathrm{out}[\operatorname{rank}(i)]=i.
\]
No full centroid sort is needed.

Selected lengths produce prefix offsets. For excess probes,
\[
 i_j=i_{n_{\rm sel}-1},\quad L_j=0\quad(j\geq n_{\rm sel}),
 \qquad\omega_{j+1}=\omega_j+L_j.
\]
Repeated IDs add no scan work. Centroid sets and probe counts must be positive.

\subsection{Costs and separate correctness contracts}

Histogram/collection reread scores; ranking costs $O(n_{\rm sel}^2)$ with growing shared storage. Small selections still pay fixed histogram allocation. The tests assess deterministic integration of this radix method.

\Cref{sec:7-4} tests ties, signed zeros, infinities, extremes and excess probes.

FP16 routing is a separate approximation in \cref{sec:7-4}, alongside cross-process identity checks.

\subsection{From database IDs to list-ordered positions}

An input row has identifier $i\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. Coarse assignment
places its transformed vector in a list according to the computed
centroid scores. The mathematical assignment target is
\begin{equation}
 a(i)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{0\leq\ell<n_{\rm list}}
       \|\Pi x_i-\mu_\ell\|_2^2.
 \label{eq:4-assignment}
\end{equation}
Its implementation uses the selected numerical assignment path. Encoding
the primary and residual representations does not subtract $\mu_{a(i)}$;
list membership restricts the future search universe independently of
those reconstructions.

The builder sorts assignments together with a sequence of input IDs.
Let $\rho(p)$ be the input ID at sorted physical position $p$ and let
$o_\ell$ be the start of list $\ell$. The completed arrays satisfy
\begin{equation}
 0=o_0\leq o_1\leq\cdots\leq o_{n_{\rm list}}=N,
 \qquad p\in[o_\ell,o_{\ell+1})\Longrightarrow a(\rho(p))=\ell.
 \label{eq:4-offsets}
\end{equation}
Lower-bound searches give offsets, with
\[
 o_\ell=o_{\ell+1}\Longleftrightarrow\text{list }\ell\text{ is empty}.
\]
Positions are stable within a snapshot, not across builds. All arrays use the same $\rho(p)$.

\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\input{figures/ch4/physical-layout}
\caption[List-ordered physical index layout]{One common physical position joins IDs, packed primary words,
residual rows and correction factors. This illustrative eight-row index
has offsets $[0,3,3,8]$, including an empty list. One word packs four subspaces of one vector; values/list sizes are schematic.}
\label{fig:4-layout}
\end{figure}

IDs map $p\mapsto\rho(p)$. Two-pass add temporarily builds $\rho^{-1}$ for scatter. Primary ties use positions; final ties use database IDs.

\subsection{Exact addresses and representation widths}

For primary byte $Z[m,p]$,
\[
 \operatorname{offset}_{\rm byte}(Z[m,p])=mN+p.
\] Final packing produces
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf w[j,p]=\sum_{t=0}^{3}2^{8t}Z[4j+t,p],\qquad
 \operatorname{addr}_{\rm byte}(\mathsf w[j,p])=4(jN+p).
 \label{eq:4-primary-address}
\end{equation}
Here $j=0,\ldots,M/4-1$. $\text{word-layout build}\Longrightarrow M\bmod4=0$; other $M$ are rejected. A separate byte-layout compilation
retains the byte representation. Each packed array occupies $NM$ bytes,
but repacking temporarily holds both old and new copies, costing $2NM$.
The one-pass builder
temporarily gathers a vector-major $[N,M]$ primary array, transposes it, and
then repacks; each obsolete copy is freed. The two-pass builder scatters
directly into the subspace-major array before the same final repack.
The search-time lane mapping is discussed in \Cref{sec:5-3}.

Residual codes remain row-major, with
$b_r=\lceil dB_r/8\rceil$ bytes per vector. In the eight-bit configuration,
coordinate $t$ of row $p$ is at byte offset $pb_r+t$. In the four-bit
path it is in byte $pb_r+\lfloor t/2\rfloor$, with even coordinates
in the low nibble and odd coordinates in the high nibble. A four-byte
correction per physical row stores
\begin{equation}
 \gamma[ p ]=2\langle\widehat p(x_{\rho(p)}),
                              \widehat r(x_{\rho(p)})\rangle.
 \label{eq:4-correction}
\end{equation}
Its value must move with that row's codes during gathering or scattering.
Residual access then reconstructs the same object that primary screening
identified, even though the two code arrays use different layouts.

Primary codes scan in list order; residual rows are fetched only for survivors. Retaining raw FP32 vectors on the device would
provide exact reranking but consume $4Nd$ additional bytes and change the
reported search design. We refine compressed reconstructions; Chapter 7 measures the resulting quality.

\subsection{Transform and sampling}

Host LAPACK QR turns a seeded Gaussian matrix into square $\Pi$. Device row-major rotation is
\begin{equation}
 Y_t=X_t\Pi^{\mathsf T},\qquad y=\Pi x,\qquad
 \|\Pi(q-x)\|_2^2=\|q-x\|_2^2
 \quad\text{when }\Pi^{\mathsf T}\Pi=I.
 \label{eq:4-transform}
\end{equation}
Dimension stays $d$; C0 checks finite-precision QR/GEMM error (\cref{sec:4-6}).

Strided primary/IVF samples use $n_t=39n_{\rm list}$: 159,744 Vogue rows, 319,488 arXiv/OpenAI rows and 1,277,952 BGE/Stella rows. This matches FAISS's warning threshold, not a quality guarantee \cite{faiss_clustering}. Residual fitting separately uses 100,000 rows.

An earlier twelve-cell Vogue/OpenAI-3072 sweep ($B_r=4/8$, probes 32/128/256) fixed primary/IVF models. At 25 Lloyd iterations, 100K rather than all rows lost at most 0.0018 recall (eleven losses, one tie); intermediate sizes were non-monotone. This supports bounded training, under that older protocol.

\subsection{Why retain the analytical primary model?}

Sample scale and Cartesian levels are
\begin{equation}
 \sigma^2=\frac{1}{n_t d}\sum_{i=0}^{n_t-1}\|x_i\|_2^2,
 \qquad D_s=d/M,\qquad K=2^B.
 \label{eq:4-scale}
\end{equation}
\[
 B=D_s=8\Longrightarrow
 \mathcal C_m=\{-a,+a\}^{8},\quad a=0.674\sigma.
\]
Eight signs occupy one byte. This JHQ structure supports $O(d)$ encoding and split LUTs \cite{jhq} (\cref{sec:5-2}); arbitrary Lloyd updates can destroy it.

For fixed sign vector $s\in\{-1,+1\}^d$,
\begin{equation}
 \|q'-a s\|^2=\|q'\|^2+da^2-2a\langle q',s\rangle.
 \label{eq:4-sign-ranking}
\end{equation}
\[
 a>0\Longrightarrow
 \arg\min_s\|q'-as\|^2=\arg\max_s\langle q',s\rangle.
\]
This real-arithmetic order is Gaussian-independent. Residuals still change with $a$; $a=0$ and FP32 ties need separate treatment.

Historical Vogue ($M=96$, $B_r=4$, 128 probes) gave primary recall 0.6618/0.6342 and full recall 0.9452/0.9409 for earlier/analytical builds. Residual training also changed, so this is not a codebook-only effect. Chapter 7 tests the full frontier.

\subsection{Coarse assignment as filter and refine}

IVF starts from spaced rotated rows and runs eight iterations, ranking $s_\ell=\|\mu_\ell\|^2-2\langle y,\mu_\ell\rangle$. Under supported dimensions, default int8 filtering resolves ambiguous assignments in FP32.

\begin{resultblock}
\begin{lemma}[Assignment with certified score intervals]
\label{lem:4-assignment-bound}
Let $\widetilde y,\widetilde\mu_\ell$ be dequantised approximations,
$e=y-\widetilde y$ and $f_\ell=\mu_\ell-\widetilde\mu_\ell$.
Keeping centroid norms exact, the approximate score
$\widetilde s_\ell=\|\mu_\ell\|^2-2\langle\widetilde y,\widetilde\mu_\ell\rangle$
has real-arithmetic error bounded by
\begin{equation}
 E_\ell=2\bigl(\|y\|\|f_\ell\|+\|e\|\|\widetilde\mu_\ell\|\bigr).
 \label{eq:4-assignment-bound}
\end{equation}
Given valid intervals $[L_\ell,U_\ell]$ containing every target score,
discarding only $L_\ell>\min_j U_j$ and exactly resolving the remaining
scores preserves the minimum and its specified tie rule.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Using $e=y-\widetilde y$ and $f_\ell=\mu_\ell-\widetilde\mu_\ell$,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \langle y,\mu_\ell\rangle-
 \langle\widetilde y,\widetilde\mu_\ell\rangle
 &=\langle y,f_\ell\rangle
   +\langle e,\widetilde\mu_\ell\rangle,\\
 |s_\ell-\widetilde s_\ell|
 &\leq2\bigl(\|y\|\|f_\ell\|
       +\|e\|\|\widetilde\mu_\ell\|\bigr)=E_\ell .
 \end{aligned}
\]
For $j^*\in\arg\min_j U_j$,
\[
 L_\ell>U_{j^*}
 \Longrightarrow
 s_\ell\geq L_\ell>U_{j^*}\geq s_{j^*}.
\]
Such $\ell$ cannot minimise the score. Equality stays eligible, preserving ties.
\end{proof}
\end{resultblock}

FP32 headroom is conservative, not a bitwise certificate without accumulation-error bounds. FP16 comparisons differ on 0/14,838 Vogue, 6/31,748 BGE and 3/16,359 Stella tail assignments. Cold logs do not identify the executed precision.

\subsection{Residual fitting and the iteration budget}

After IVF, residuals remain $r=\Pi x-\widehat p(x)$. Each subspace fits $K_r=2^{B_r}$ sorted scalar levels shared across coordinates, using GPU sorting/Lloyd updates capped at 2,000.

Historical 100K samples gained 0.0063--0.0076 recall from 25$\to$2,000 updates. Tail bins and BGE/Stella changes persisted, so reaching the cap does not establish convergence or contradict exact Lloyd descent. At 20,000 updates, historical Stella all-row/100K recall was 0.9921/0.9920.

\subsection{Construction work and observed imbalance}

\[
 W_{\rm QR}=O(d^3),\qquad W_{\rm rotate}=O(n_t d^2).
\]
Direct coarse assignment costs $O(n_t n_{\rm list}d)$ per iteration.
\[
 W_{\rm primary}=O(MKD_s),\qquad
 W_{\rm residual\ extraction}=O(n_rd),
\]
followed by sorting and scalar updates. These describe work, rather than predict latency.
Synchronised phase diagnostics place about 83\% of BGE/Stella training
in IVF k-means (about 2.97\,s). They use one add buffer and forced
synchronisation, separately from the normal overlapped timings in
\cref{sec:7-7}.


List-size imbalance enters the scan rule in \cref{sec:5-5}. The
individual contributions of eight IVF iterations, spaced seeds and
finite sampling to that imbalance were not isolated.


\paragraph{Arithmetic used in the measured implementation.}
The evaluated implementation (v69) stores FP32 matrices but enables cuBLAS
TF32 tensor-core math for $d\geq1{,}536$. In its compiled faithful branch,
a null override falls through to the dimension-based default. This affects
training/add/query rotation and centroid GEMMs on both OpenAI datasets;
an environment override cannot disable that branch. Thus FP32 storage does
not imply full FP32 multiplication. The supplementary FP32 variant (v72)
corrects this switch. Its sensitivity experiment reuses the same
TF32-trained cache and changes add/query arithmetic, rather than retraining
the model in FP32 (\cref{sec:7-precision}).

\subsection{Bounded input batches and two-pass construction}

Whole-database raw/rotated storage is $4Nd+4Nd=8Nd$ bytes. Bounded staging avoids it. For $n_b$ pipeline
buffers, configured add rows $a_{\rm add}$ and per-array byte budget
$S_{\rm stage}$, the source stages
\begin{equation}
 a_{\rm in}=\max\!\left\{1,\min\!\left(a_{\rm add},
 \left\lfloor\frac{S_{\rm stage}}{4d}\right\rfloor\right)\right\},
 \qquad S_{\rm float}=8n_ba_{\rm in}d.
 \label{eq:4-staging-rows}
\end{equation}
\[
 4d\leq S_{\rm stage},\quad n_b=3,\ S_{\rm stage}=128\,\mathrm{MiB}
 \Longrightarrow S_{\rm float}\leq2n_bS_{\rm stage}=768\,\mathrm{MiB}.
\]
Assignment/encoder scratch is additional.

One-pass add gathers encoded input-order arrays, keeping both copies briefly. Two-pass add assigns/sorts first, then re-reads and scatters encodings directly. It saves simultaneous storage at the cost of another rotation/read; raw assignment against back-rotated centroids uses orthogonality.

\subsection{Phase occupancy and the process peak}

The one-pass estimate is
\begin{equation}
 H_{\rm single}=N(2b_r+3M+20)+2^{30}\quad\text{bytes}.
 \label{eq:4-peak-heuristic}
\end{equation}
Its ten live arrays sum to
\[
 3NM+2Nb_r+20N=N(3M+2b_r+20).
\]
The added 1\,GiB is heuristic headroom, not a whole-process peak bound.

Final two-pass repack counts IDs, residuals, corrections and two primary copies:
\begin{equation}
 S_{\rm repack,2}=N(b_r+2M+8).
 \label{eq:4-two-pass-repack}
\end{equation}
 Whole-build peak also considers earlier pipeline/inverse scratch, model, sort, context and later workspace allocations.

\frontchapter{Abstract}
JHQ-GPU runs JHQ's primary/residual search on a GPU. It combines index construction, packed scanning, lane refinement and workload-level calibration. Cartesian splitting replaces 256 LUT entries with $16+16$, giving a storage ratio $32/256=1/8$ with the same real-arithmetic score. Calibration compares sampled top-$k$ IDs with a larger-budget reference, without GT or a learned predictor.

On six RTX 5090 datasets, two-group LUTs lead in 22/24 cells; the largest index holds 17.78 million vectors at 20.44\,GiB resident memory. Full-pool calibration meets a $10^{-3}$ held-out
recall-loss target relative to the best tested budget in 12/12 cells, with
maximum loss 0.0006; smaller samples expose workload-dependent quality risk.
At recall 0.97 and batch 1,000, JHQ leads in three of four datasets and is
near parity with IVF-RaBitQ on arXiv. OpenAI runs use TF32; FP32 checks
retain favourable comparisons under a TF32-trained cache. At batch 8 and
the same recall, CAGRA fp32 leads on all four datasets. These results
locate the execution, quality and capacity trade-offs of GPU JHQ.
